text: In representing the Municipal Corporation, I argued before the Supreme Court that the lower courts fell into serious error by decreeing the respondents' suit based solely on a mutation entry, without the plaintiffs even joining the actual sellers as parties or proving any payment of consideration. Furthermore, the corporation has always maintained physical possession of the property and collected rent from the shops situated thereon. We also contested belated attempts by third parties to join the proceedings after decades of slumber. Although we brought our historic ownership records forward, the apex court ultimately disposed of the matter without relying on those documents, and we are now seeking a review of how the lower concurrent findings were allowed to stand.

As the rightful owners who acquired the property through official mutation entries, we had to approach the civil court because the local municipal administration wrongfully withheld possession and denied our title. Every lower court thoroughly reviewed the record and upheld our ownership, noting that the corporation failed to prove any lawful claim. Even when the administration and an intervening claimant attempted to stall our victory at the highest judicial forum with untimely petitions and new papers, we maintained that our status as legitimate buyers without notice was unassailable.

We legally bought our land and got our names entered in the official ownership records years ago, but the local municipal office refused to hand over possession and kept taking rent from the shops built there. We won our case in every single lower court because the officials could never prove the land belonged to them. Later, some random person and the municipal corporation tried bringing up old auction claims and forgotten papers in the highest court after staying quiet for over fifty years, but those tricks did not work.

My client originally approached the civil court seeking a formal declaration of ownership, recovery of possession, and a permanent injunction regarding jointly held property after family shares were disturbed. Although the trial judge ruled in our favour, the High Court overturned that decision, ruling that the matter was barred under procedural rules and limitation. Before this apex court, we argued that our initial approach to the revenue authorities and subsequent litigation fell well within permissible time limits, especially since matters were already sub-judice. However, the Supreme Court has unfortunately ruled against us, concluding that our primary declaration plea crossed the six-year statutory limit from the date of the disputed property transfer, thereby invalidating all consequential remedies.

On behalf of the appellant, we challenged the High Court's adverse finding which had dismissed our civil revision regarding joint land rights. We maintained that our legal action was timely, having first contested the wrongful property transfer before the revenue hierarchy and later seeking civil intervention when those administrative remedies proved ineffective. We urged that the limitation clock should not defeat our legitimate property claim. Regrettably, the highest court has now dismissed our appeal, holding that our primary request for a declaration of title was instituted fourteen years after the mutation entry, thus breaching the six-year window prescribed by the Limitation Act and rendering any dependent reliefs legally ineffective.

We defended our lawful acquisition of the property against the appellant's belated claims. The opposing party initiated a civil lawsuit nearly fourteen years after the disputed property mutation was officially sanctioned, despite earlier awareness and separate legal actions concerning other land parcels. Both the High Court and now the Supreme Court agreed with our stance that the main relief for ownership declaration was hopelessly time-barred under the governing limitation laws. Because the principal claim was filed far beyond the permissible six-year period, the Supreme Court rightly dismissed their entire appeal, affirming that all consequential requests for possession and injunction must fall along with it.

We joined the police force years ahead of him and completed all our required training courses and exams long before he did. He tried to claim seniority over us and got a favorable order from the tribunal, which wasn't fair because we earned our promotions through seniority and hard work. The police department took the matter to the highest court, and thankfully the judges agreed that he wasn't our senior, setting aside that wrong tribunal order.

In representing my client who contested for the National Assembly constituency, I filed an appeal against the improper dismissal of our election petition by the tribunal below. We challenged the victory of the returned candidate pointing out serious electoral irregularities across 104 polling stations where our polling agents were blocked from entry and fake votes were cast. Additionally, our applications for checking counterfoils through NADRA's biometric system and recounting thousands of rejected votes were wrongly turned down. The tribunal failed to appreciate the gravity of these matters. Unfortunately, the apex court upheld the lower forum's decision and dismissed our appeal, ruling that our material was insufficient to prove corrupt practices.

As counsel for the appellant, I urged the apex court to review the erroneous findings of the election tribunal which had dismissed our challenge against the successful candidate in NA-266. We demonstrated that out of numerous voting booths, a significant portion witnessed systematic manipulation, locking out our representatives and stuffing fake ballots. We also sought verification of counterfoils and a recount of an unusually high number of rejected ballots, requests that the tribunal had unjustly rejected. We argued that these steps would expose the massive rigging. Regrettably, the Supreme Court maintained the tribunal's order and dismissed the case, holding that the allegations lacked concrete substantiation.

I am the respondent who won the election from the National Assembly constituency with a clear majority of votes, but my opponent dragged me into endless litigation by filing a baseless election petition. He claimed widespread rigging and manipulation at numerous polling booths without presenting any credible proof or lodging complaints with authorities at the relevant time. The election tribunal rightly threw out his petition and subsequently dismissed his requests for biometric verification and recounting. My legal team successfully established that the high count of rejected votes was due to a candidate being disqualified after ballot papers were printed. The Supreme Court agreed with our stance, affirming the tribunal's verdict and dismissing his appeal completely.

We defended our electoral victory against the unfounded accusations brought by the runner-up candidate before the election tribunal. My opponent alleged various corrupt practices and tried to block the results by demanding biometric checks and vote recounts, all of which the lower tribunal found meritless and dismissed. We pointed out that his own witnesses admitted during cross-examination that they never raised any official objections on polling day. Furthermore, the disputed figure of rejected ballots was simply the result of a disqualified candidate's name remaining on the printed papers. The Supreme Court upheld the lower court decisions and dismissed the appellant's challenge, endorsing our lawful win.

Our candidate lost the election because the winners indulged in massive cheating and kept our agents away from many voting booths. We knocked on the doors of the election tribunal asking for a proper check of the voting records and rejected papers, but they dismissed everything we said. We then took the matter to the Supreme Court hoping for justice, but they also turned us down and dismissed the case, stating that our complaints were too general and lacked solid evidence.

My client narrowly won the election after a fiercely contested race, but his opponent challenged the outcome through an election petition. However, that petition suffered from a fatal legal flaw right from its inception: it was filed, verified, and presented not by the petitioner himself, but through an attorney, in direct violation of the mandatory requirements of the relevant electoral laws which demand personal verification by the candidate. Although we raised this objection in our written statement and the Tribunal framed a specific issue regarding it, the lower forum brushed it aside and ordered a re-poll across the entire constituency. We challenged that decision before the Supreme Court, arguing that bypassing statutory mandates renders the petition non-maintainable. The apex court agreed with our contentions, allowed our appeal, and set aside the flawed judgment of the Tribunal.

As counsel for the appellant, I approached the Supreme Court against the decision of the Election Tribunal which had nullified my client's electoral victory and ordered fresh elections in the whole constituency. Our primary legal ground was that the opposing candidate's election petition was legally dead on arrival because it was filed and verified through an attorney instead of the candidate himself, violating clear and mandatory statutory provisions. The Tribunal had erroneously overlooked this legal bar and entertained the defective challenge. We urged the highest court to rectify this error. The Supreme Court accepted our appeal, held that the petition was not maintainable due to the lack of mandatory personal verification, and overturned the Tribunal's ruling entirely.

After I lost the election by a very narrow margin, I noticed serious irregularities and questionable counting regarding invalid ballots that wrongly favored my opponent. Seeking justice, I approached the Election Tribunal through my designated attorney to question the validity of the polls. The Tribunal examined the record, agreed with our contentions, and rightfully struck down the notification of the returned candidate, ordering fresh polling across the constituency. However, my opponent took the matter to the Supreme Court, raising technical objections about my attorney filing and verifying the petition instead of me doing it personally. The apex court accepted their appeal and set aside the Tribunal's favorable verdict, holding that the petition was not maintainable due to this procedural requirement.

We fought hard during the elections, but our opponent won by a tiny margin after some suspicious counting. We filed a formal challenge through our legal helper, and the tribunal judge listened to us and ordered re-polling for the whole area. Sadly, the winner appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the petition was invalid because our leader didn't sign it personally. The Supreme Court ruled in their favor, canceling the tribunal's order.

My client, the appellant company, holds numerous prior registered trade marks for the brand dating back decades across various categories, including the specific class in dispute. We challenged the lower tribunals' rulings that allowed the opposing party to register an identical brand name based on an old business arrangement from 1975. We argued that the historic agreement never transferred proprietary rights or permitted brand appropriation, and that the opposing party failed to prove its corporate succession despite being granted ample opportunity by the apex court. The Supreme Court accepted our contentions, ruling that the rival mark lacked distinctiveness, violated statutory prohibitions against confusingly similar marks, and set aside all previous unfavorable decisions.

As counsel for the appellant enterprise, I challenged the Sindh High Court's verdict which had endorsed the trade mark registrar's order favoring the respondents. We demonstrated before the apex bench that our client is the original proprietor holding dozens of valid registrations for the contested brand since the nineteen fifties. The respondents attempted to claim rights through a restrictive 1975 operational accord, yet failed to establish their legal succession or submit mandatory corporate documents when directed. The Supreme Court agreed that allowing the registration would mislead consumers and breached statutory protections, ultimately setting aside the lower court judgments in our favor.

Our company has operated our restaurant and food business for years based on a valid agreement made decades ago that handed over the goodwill of these shops to us. We applied to register our name officially, and the trade mark officials as well as the High Court agreed that we had every right to use it in our region. Another company tried to block us by claiming older rights, but we defended our hard-earned business identity through all the legal forums.

My client, the Federation of Pakistan through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, challenged the rulings of the Federal Service Tribunal which had entertained and accepted service appeals from individuals who were hired locally by our diplomatic missions abroad. We maintained that these staff members, being engaged on a temporary or contract basis by the respective Heads of Missions under specific financial management rules for foreign missions, do not fall within the legal definition of civil servants under the Civil Servants Act. Consequently, the Service Tribunal lacked the requisite jurisdiction to hear their grievances. The Supreme Court accepted our arguments, set aside the tribunal's decisions, and ruled in our favor by holding that contract-based local employees cannot invoke service tribunal jurisdiction.

As counsel for the appellant authorities, I argued before the Supreme Court that the Service Tribunal committed a grave error of law by granting relief to individuals who were locally recruited by our embassies and consulates abroad. These personnel were hired purely on a contractual footing pursuant to the financial guidelines governing foreign missions, meaning they are explicitly excluded from the category of civil servants under statutory law. The lower tribunal had no legal competence to adjudicate their employment disputes. The apex court agreed with our stance, overturning the impugned judgments and upholding the principle that locally engaged mission staff cannot approach the service tribunal.

We were appointed to regular sanctioned positions within the Ministry of Foreign Affairs while working at Pakistani missions overseas, serving for many years before our employment was abruptly terminated. We approached the Federal Service Tribunal because we considered ourselves civil servants entitled to statutory protections against arbitrary removal. Although the government argued that our local recruitment contracts placed us outside civil servant laws, the tribunal accepted our appeals and found in our favor. However, the government has now challenged that relief in the Supreme Court, insisting that our contractual status as locally engaged staff bars us from seeking remedy before the service tribunal.

We had to challenge the tribunal's decision because people who are hired locally on contracts at our foreign embassies keep filing cases as if they are regular government servants. They are not civil servants under the law, and the service tribunal had no business interfering in their contract terminations. The highest court understood our point and set aside those wrong judgments so that foreign mission rules are properly respected.

We are being dragged into unnecessary litigation over land that rightfully belongs to our family through inheritance. A distant claimant suddenly appeared decades later, claiming the property was given to her as a wedding gift, even though she never approached the proper family forums or updated the official revenue registers on time. Lower judges examined the facts and decided in our favor, recognizing that her claims were hopelessly late and legally flawed.

My clients filed this appeal to challenge the Sindh High Court's decision that wrongly restored the trial court's decree in favor of the original owners' children. We maintained throughout that the property was legally bought by intermediaries who then sold it to my clients. The first judge agreed with us and dismissed the plaintiffs' claim, but the appellate judge reversed it. Then the High Court ignored our evidence regarding the land mutation and wrongly concluded that the sale wasn't proved. We argue the High Court misread the evidence and that the opposing suit was barred by time. However, the Supreme Court ultimately dismissed our appeal, holding that we failed to substantiate the original sale transactions through proper documents or witnesses.

My clients approached the High Court seeking implementation of the provincial regularization law passed in 2013, along with their pending salary dues. However, the High Court committed grave judicial overreach by declaring that beneficial statute void without any challenge to its validity being raised before it, thereby exercising unconstitutional suo motu powers. Furthermore, the impugned judgment abruptly reversed the regularization status of numerous employees who were not even parties to the litigation and had no opportunity to defend themselves. We appealed this flawed decision to the Supreme Court, which agreed with our contentions, set aside the High Court's ruling, and remanded the matter back for a proper, fair hearing of all concerned parties.

After serving as legal officers for a long time, we expected our jobs to be regularized under the provincial law enacted for contract employees. Instead, the court dismissed our petitions and unexpectedly issued sweeping orders that ruined the service records of hundreds of innocent colleagues without ever listening to them. We challenged this injustice before the Supreme Court, which agreed that the lower court acted improperly, cancelled its ruling, and sent the whole matter back down to be decided properly from scratch.

As counsel for the appellant in this service matter, I argued before the apex court that my client, previously employed as a time scale clerk, was unjustly penalized by the department through increment stoppage and financial recovery directives based on a flawed fact-finding process. Furthermore, the departmental appellate authority modified the initial penalty, yet the Federal Service Tribunal completely ignored this crucial appellate order in its dismissal judgment. We stressed that no proper witnesses were examined in my client's presence and that the main culprit, Muhammad Amin Khan, had already confessed to the entire fraud and deposited the misappropriated funds himself. The Supreme Court accepted our arguments, set aside the flawed Tribunal judgment, and remanded the case back for a fresh and thorough hearing.

Representing the aggrieved civil servant before the Supreme Court, I challenged the Federal Service Tribunal's decision that upheld departmental penalties imposed on my client regarding alleged pension fund discrepancies. We pointed out that the tribunal failed to evaluate the actual inquiry report or the confession made by the co-accused, Muhammad Amin Khan, who took full responsibility for the embezzlement and was subsequently convicted by a criminal court. The tribunal also overlooked the modifications made during the departmental appeal. Finding merit in our contentions regarding the denial of a fair opportunity to defend and the lack of proper scrutiny of evidence, the Supreme Court set aside the lower tribunal's ruling and sent the matter back for a fresh decision.

As the respondent department defending our administrative actions before the apex court, we maintained that serious financial irregularities involving pension disbursements occurred under the watch of the appellant, who served as a time scale clerk. We argued that during the internal inquiry, his negligence and failure to follow proper procedures contributed significantly to the massive shortfall of funds. Although the initial penalty was later modified on his departmental appeal, we maintained that the disciplinary action was entirely justified based on his failure to properly handle government money. The Supreme Court, however, decided to set aside the service tribunal's previous dismissal and sent the dispute back for a fresh review.

We defended the department's position before the Supreme Court, asserting that the penalties of financial recovery and scale reduction imposed on the employee were fully warranted due to grave irregularities discovered during our verification checks of pension payments. We contended that the inquiry established his responsibility for failing to secure proper receipts and oversight while dealing with public funds. The service tribunal had initially upheld the department's disciplinary stance. However, the Supreme Court has now annulled that tribunal decision and directed that the service appeal be reheard from scratch.

My client challenged the concurrent findings of the lower forums where his civil suit was nonsuited on technical grounds. We argued that our initial grievance was actively pursued before the revenue authorities within the statutory timeframe following the disputed mutation entry. The trial court had rightly understood our entitlement under the joint family holding, but the High Court erred in applying procedural bars like Order II Rule 2 and limitation laws. We maintained that the ongoing administrative proceedings kept our cause alive. However, the apex court ruled against us, holding that our principal prayer for ownership declaration was brought fourteen years after the transfer, crossing the six-year limitation threshold, which consequently killed all ancillary reliefs.

My client challenged the election outcome for the National Assembly constituency after losing to the opposing candidate by a narrow margin. We filed an election petition pointing out widespread irregularities, including the exclusion of our polling agents from numerous polling booths, an intimidating environment created by supporters of the returned candidate, and the rampant casting of fake ballots. During the proceedings, we moved applications seeking NADRA biometric verification of counterfoils and a recount of the massive number of rejected ballots, but the Tribunal turned them down and eventually dismissed our petition. We then approached the apex court arguing that the lower forum erred by ignoring our requests for verifying election data. Unfortunately, the Supreme Court upheld the lower tribunal's decision and dismissed our appeal, ruling that our material was insufficient.

I am representing the candidate who contested the general elections for the national legislature seat but was declared runner-up against the respondent. Our initial challenge before the election tribunal detailed how illegal practices and systematic rigging marred polling at over a hundred stations, where our representatives were barred from entering. We requested the tribunal to order a fingerprint check through biometric databases and to recount the heavily inflated rejected votes, but both pleas were rejected, and the tribunal threw out our petition. In our appeal before the highest judicial forum, we contended that these investigative steps were vital to uncover the truth. Regrettably, the Supreme Court dismissed our appeal, maintaining that the evidence produced was too general to warrant interference.

We won the general election for the national assembly seat fairly, securing the highest tally of votes with a comfortable lead. My opponent filed a challenge before the election tribunal accusing us of widespread rigging and illegal acts, claiming his agents were kept away from booths. The tribunal thoroughly examined the matter and dismissed his petition because he failed to produce any concrete proof or witnesses to support his vague claims. He then took the matter to the highest court, insisting on biometric checks and vote recounts. We defended our victory by pointing out that the large count of invalid votes was due to a disqualified candidate whose name remained on the ballot papers. Ultimately, the Supreme Court agreed with our stance and dismissed his appeal, cementing our legitimate win.

As the winning candidate, I defended my electoral victory against the allegations brought forward by my rival. He filed a petition alleging that widespread manipulation and corrupt practices took place during the voting process. The election tribunal dismissed his claims, noting they were merely broad assertions lacking solid documentary proof or credible testimony. Unhappy with that ruling, he approached the Supreme Court to overturn the decision and order biometric verification along with a vote recount. We argued before the bench that his witnesses admitted they never lodged any official complaints during or after the polling. The Supreme Court dismissed his appeal, ruling that his allegations were unsubstantiated and that our election was legally sound.

As counsel for the aggrieved civil servant, I argued before the apex court that the Service Tribunal committed a grave error by dismissing my client's service appeal without examining the core evidence or the impact of the departmental appellate order. My client was penalized for a financial shortfall in pension payments even though the actual perpetrator had openly confessed in writing to the fraud, deposited restitution funds, and received a criminal conviction. Furthermore, no proper witness examination or cross-examination took place during the flawed inquiry proceedings, denying my client a fair defense. The Supreme Court agreed with our position, nullified the dismissal order, and sent the matter back to the Tribunal for a fresh decision after proper scrutiny.

As representatives of the postal administration, we maintained throughout the proceedings that the employee was rightly held accountable for failing to perform his duties properly, which allowed financial discrepancies to occur in pension accounts. The department followed all due procedures, and after considering his reply, imposed a justified penalty that was subsequently reviewed and adjusted by the appellate authority. Although the Service Tribunal supported our stance and dismissed his appeal, the Supreme Court has intervened, setting aside the Tribunal's order and remanding the matter back so the panel can reconsider the entire inquiry report and the statements of all involved parties afresh.
